summary.text: 汽 combines the water element 氵 with 气 as a sound element. Earlier dictionary accounts gloss it as “water dried up,” with “tears falling” as an alternative; later records also give “water vapor,” and modern use commonly includes compounds for vapor and gasoline. The path between these meanings is not documented here.

formation.text: The supported analysis is phonosemantic: water supplies the meaning category, while 气 supplies the sound. A secondary proposal treats 气 as meaning “air,” so that the two parts suggest steam; the evidence here does not establish that as an additional original intention.

components.text: 氵 is the conventional side form of 水 and contributes the water category. The reported older senses are “water dried up” and, alternatively, “tears falling”; no historical glyph image was available here to verify the form’s earlier graphic appearance.

气 is the sound-bearing part in the dictionary’s analysis. A modern sound comparison is available, and a historical reconstruction reports the same form for both characters; this supports, but does not independently prove, the component analysis.

sound.text: Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese is reported as *kʰɯds for both 汽 and 气, a within-system comparison consistent with the phonetic analysis.

history.text: The inspected dictionary account reproduces an analysis attributed to Shuowen and reports a small-seal form, but its image was not visually inspected. No earlier graphic sequence or evidence of corruption is established here.

The accounts distinguish the older glosses from the later distribution: modern 汽 specializes in uses such as water vapor and gasoline, while 汔 is said to carry the older senses. The evidence does not date or explain this written-form distribution.

uncertainties.text: The available evidence supports water plus 气 as sound element. The alternative “water plus air” interpretation is a secondary proposal, and the evidence does not show whether it was also intended when the graph was formed.
The vapor sense is reported through Jiyun, but its earliest attestation and its semantic connection, if any, to “water dried up” or “tears falling” are not established here.

No inspected source dates the shift in dominant use or explains when and how the older senses came to be written with 汔. The Shijing phrase is reported, but its original written form is not established here.

senses.text: An older dictionary account glosses 汽 as “water dried up.” The available evidence does not date this use, so it cannot be identified here as the earliest attested meaning.
“Tears falling” is recorded as an alternative older gloss; its chronology relative to the other senses is unresolved.
A dictionary reports “water vapor” through Jiyun. The inspected evidence does not date that attestation.

senses.gloss: vapor and gas in modern compounds
senses.text: Modern 汽 is used in compounds for water vapor and gasoline. This compound evidence supports current usage but does not make the compound meanings independent single-character senses.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish a semantic path from drying or tears to water vapor, nor does it date the shift in dominant use. The dictionary’s report that 汔 now carries older senses does not establish a dated borrowing or reassignment process.

overview.text: 汽 uses 氵 to mark the water category and 气 as a sound element. Older dictionary glosses include “water dried up”; the common modern use concerns vapor and compounds such as those for gasoline.

components.text: 氵 is the water side form, marking the relevant meaning category.
气 is the sound-bearing element in the supported analysis.

relationships.text: In 汽, 氵 represents the water meaning category; it is the side form of 水.
The older dictionary analysis identifies 气 as the sound element. Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese reports *kʰɯds for both 气 and 汽, a within-system comparison consistent with that role.
